That's going to feed into this narrative that the government is too chummy with AI companies and that AI companies are not acting in good faith when it comes to policy issues. And so I think a better way to go about this is not for the government to sort of provide an anti-trust exemption, but rather to facilitate or lead or coordinate these conversations and ensure that they're not sort of bilateral conversations happening between two companies who then set the rules for everyone else, but that there's a big tent where we see a lot of players in the AI ecosystem have a voice and then figure out a way to proceed that doesn't just reflect or appear to reflect the preferences of these two companies that are clearly in the lead when it comes to model capabilities. You know, it's hard to say. I do think there's some evidence that China or Chinese policymakers have some of the same concerns that we see with US policymakers, where they see where AI technology is going, particularly around cyber capabilities. And they think about whether it is okay to have all of those capabilities publicly available. And so there's, you know, at least some discussions internally within China about whether future Chinese frontier models should be provided openly or if there should be restricted access to them in some way, perhaps to select groups of organizations like we've seen with some of the powerful US models or maybe only available within China. I think they are concerned. And maybe a little bit of optimism. We know AI is going to be on the agenda for this looming summit that the US and China are going to have. They committed to discussing AI topics at their last summit. And so, you know, there's at least a possibility that there could be some significant discussions and advancements on this topic. But what I really worry about is that we're entering this realm of self-fulfilling prophecy, where a lot of the rhetoric around China is they're distilling US models, they're not really good at AI, they're just sort of stealing intellectual property from US companies, combined with, you know, suggestions that the US is asking countries to take sides and either use US technology or Chinese technology, plus export controls, plus even thoughts about banning or restricting access to Chinese open-away models. All of these are really antagonizing towards China, really sort of puts them in the mindset of being an enemy. And this makes it really hard to have productive conversations. And my personal belief is that you can have productive conversations, that you can restrict those conversations to a narrow set of issues that relate to AI safety, that relate to agreement on definitions, the creation of communication channels, maybe in, you know, ways to share information about AI cyber incidents. And that you could do this in a way that is minimally restrictive on each country's respective AI companies, that affects them in similar ways, that doesn't interfere with the ability of the US and China to compete for AI adoption globally on the merits of their technology. But that doing so requires sort of engaging with China in good faith on this narrow set of issues and setting the conditions for having a productive conversation. And then as a follow-up, figuring out, because I think it's going to be very hard to get the US and China to trust each other's claims, to figure out some sort of formal verification mechanism so you don't have to rely on the word of the other company, that there are ways to guarantee the veracity of information that each country is providing to the other. And look, I acknowledge those are really, really hard problems, that the current political and economic context makes them even more challenging. But I do think there is a narrow path to have these kinds of conversations, and that if we aren't able to do that, that it would be overall better for most people in the world. Yeah, certainly.
